messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Kofi's Vigil

Kofi Mensah was thirty-four years old when the Humvee ahead of his convoy detonated on a dusty road outside Kandahar. He had been stationed there for seven months, long enough to know the landscape's deceptive patterns—which orchards harbored IEDs, which village elders could be trusted, which silences meant danger. The blast threw his vehicle sideways. For a moment, everything was sound and dust and the copper smell of blood mixing with scorched metal and diesel fuel. Then came the screaming. His gunner, Martinez, was screaming. Kofi's hands moved through the motions of trauma care—tourniquet, pressure, radio—but Martinez died anyway, there in the back of the vehicle, while Kofi knelt beside him unable to do enough, unable to do anything that mattered.

That was twelve years ago. Now, at forty-six, Kofi worked as a park ranger in the Cascade Range, a job he had chosen deliberately for its solitude and its clear sight lines. He had married his high school sweetheart, Diana, five years after returning home. She loved him, or loved the version of him she could still reach. The man who came back from Afghanistan was not quite the man who left.

The triggers had calcified into the architecture of his daily life. A helicopter passing overhead—there were several flight paths over the park for search and rescue and ranger operations—would send Kofi into an immediate state of hyperalertness. His body would tense, his breathing would shallow, and for several seconds he would be certain that something catastrophic was about to unfold. The feeling would pass, but only after his mind had already catalogued every exit, every piece of cover, every potential threat in his vicinity. Sometimes, during these moments, he would feel himself beginning to float away from his own body, as though he were watching himself from a distance. These dissociative episodes frightened him more than the initial panic because they made him feel untethered, unreal, as though the ground beneath him might not be solid.

But the helicopter sounds were just the obvious triggers. What had come to dominate Kofi's existence was a more pervasive discomfort—a constant low-grade unease that had no clear source. It was the feeling of being unsafe in his own skin. He had come to believe that his body itself was the problem, that something fundamental had broken in him on that road and would never repair. When he was alone in the backcountry for his ranger patrols, he felt this discomfort most acutely, a creeping sense that he was fundamentally damaged, permanently changed into someone lesser than he had been before.

The memory of the blast was not something Kofi had to actively recall—it lived in his sensory world unbidden. The smell of diesel and blood would arise without warning, sometimes triggered by nothing more than the scent of a barbecue or road tar warming in the sun. When the memories did surface fully, they felt more vivid and immediate than anything happening around him. He could see the exact pattern of dust particles in the light streaming through the vehicle's window. He could see Martinez's face. These memories were so clear, so three-dimensional, that they often felt more real than the actual present moment.

Diana had noticed the changes first. Kofi watched people too carefully now, especially men he didn't know. At the grocery store, at church, at the ranger station—he observed them with an intensity that made others uncomfortable. He was always scanning, always assessing, his eyes never still. When an unexpected sound occurred, he went rigid. Diana had learned not to approach him from behind. He had nearly struck her once when she touched his shoulder while he was looking out the window.

What tormented Kofi most was the guilt. He replayed the moment of the blast endlessly, searching for what he could have done differently. If he had been driving faster, perhaps the timing would have been altered. If he had noticed something in the road, some subtle sign he had missed. If he had somehow been able to save Martinez despite the severity of the injuries, despite the impossible physics of the situation. He had come to believe that his inability to prevent that death, his fundamental failure in that moment, was something he would never forgive himself for. The belief had hardened into certainty.

Three weeks ago, Diana had found him sitting in the garage at two in the morning, unable to explain why he was there. She had finally insisted he call someone. Kofi had resisted for days, but the discomfort had become unbearable, and the guilt had begun to feel like a weight that might crush him entirely. He was afraid that if he didn't find help, he might disappear into that floating, unreal feeling and never come back. He was hoping that someone could help him understand whether the man he had become was truly irreversible, or whether there was some part of Kofi Mensah that could still be salvaged.
